newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end higher helped by bonds.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end higher helped by bonds.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended slightly higher Tuesday, helped by sharply higher U.S. bond prices and a weaker U.S. dollar, after U.S. economic data suggested the Federal Reserve may not raise interest rates again in May.

"The lower dollar and interest rates today could shift the scenario if the Federal Reserve really does refrain from tightening further, but in the meantime funds are heavily short in gold and the trade is looking for lower prices," said analyst Scott Meyers of Pioneer Futures in New York.

U.S. March durable goods orders fell 3.0 percent, the largest drop since August 1996, while the first quarter employment cost index rose 0.6 percent, less than the consensus forecast rise of 0.9 percent.
The threat of higher real interest rates and the strong U.S. dollar has been deterring investors from seeing value in precious metals, analysts said.
COMEX June gold ended up 20 cents at $341.60 an ounce, after trading a $340.80-342.20 range. Estimated total volume in COMEX gold was moderate at 19,000 lots.

Despite Monday's sharp fall in gold prices, COMEX June gold continued to hold above its contract low seen on April 16 at $339.50, analysts noted, and there was little follow through selling Tuesday, prompting some light shortcovering.

In the bullion market spot gold ended quoted $339.70/20, after fixing in London Tuesday afternoon at $339.25. Earlier spot gold had fixed Tuesday morning at $338.95, the lowest since February 12 this year when four year lows were seen.
But the fear of further official gold sales continues to hang over the market, with Swiss Finance Minister, Kaspar Villiger, reported to be lifting his opposition to IMF gold sales in news Tuesday.

Some analysts also believe central bank activity has been behind the renewed slide in gold prices in the past two months, as commodity funds have been relatively inactive in gold until the past two weeks, and short term implied gold lease rates have remained below 1.00 percent.
But funds are now heavily net short gain in COMEX gold, according to the latest CFTC Commitment of Traders data.
"Non-commercial" net short positions rose to 37,500 lots as of April 22, up from 18,882 lots two weeks earlier, and the net short position is now near last year's record levels.
But gold prices around current levels are starting to test industry economics, which could be bullish longer term, analysts said.
The price of gold in South African rand is back down to the lows seen in February around 1500 rand, while in Australian dollars gold is at its lowest level for at least 10 years at A$435 an ounce.

Of the six South African mining houses that have reported profits for the first quarter so far, only one has seen profits increase, and some analysts think many South African mining houses will be running at a loss in the second quarter.
The world's largest gold producer, Anglo American Corp of South Africa has warned of shaft closure at two of its mines.
COMEX July silver, now the active contract, ended up 1.2 cent at $4.67 an ounce, after seeing a $4.645-4.695 intraday range. Estimated total volume in COMEX silver was a high 41,000 lots.
Earlier in London spot silver fixed at $4.6425, its lowest in two years, following the slide COMEX July silver to a new contract low at $4.630 on Monday.
"Silver has seen some very heavy fund liquidation in recent weeks, but now looks to be settling down into a narrow trading range of $4.90-4.60 basis spot," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said.
The latest CFTC showed funds moving from a net long position of 3,258 lots two weeks ago, to a net short position of 384 lots as of April 22.

NYMEX July platinum closed up $1.10 at $373.60, while NYMEX June palladium gained $1.20 to $157.50, with little progress seen this week on a resumption of Russian PGM supplies to Japan under its annual contract.
In the physical market, one month platinum and palladium remained in backwardation, with lease rates quoted around 15 percent and platinum around 8 percent, refining sources said.
But Japanese palladium imports in the first quarter 1996 amounted to 26.81 tonnes, up from 20.54 tonnes in the same quarter last year, with most supplies still said to be of Russian origin.

But analysts said the material may have been hallmarked of "Russian" origin, but it probably came from world inventories, as PGM lease rates in the physical market were still high, and refiners said there had been no Russian offers noted in the spot market recently.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641))
